Learn to hear the bahr

Urdu poetry is sung in bahrs — patterns of long and short syllables. This app teaches you to hear them, see them, and scan them for yourself.

Weight

How long each syllable is — the raw material of every meter.

Words we use

miṣraʿ
A single line or hemistich of poetry.
sheʿr
A complete, self-contained two-line couplet.
baḥr
The meter or rhythmic pattern that a poem follows.
rukn
A metrical foot (e.g. mafāʿīlun, fāʿilātun).
dum / da
Vocal mnemonics for long (=) and short (–) syllables.

Letters & weight

Three rules. A syllable is two letters or one. It starts with a consonant if it can. The split follows pronunciation.

The weight law. Two letters → long (=). One letter → short (–).

Invisible to meter: zer/zabar/pesh, the aspiration ھ, the nasal ں. Counts: hamza ء and ع as full consonants; tashdīd doubles its letter; آ is two letters.

Special cases

A few words split differently than the three rules alone would predict.

Bending

Flexibility in Urdu prosody. Many common monosyllables (کو، سے، کا، ہے، میں، بھی، نے، ہوں، یہ، وہ، جو، تو) can count as long (=) or short (–) according to the requirement of the meter.

Final vowels before vowels, the Persian iẓāfat connector (ِ / -e), and the conjunction o ("and") bridge words or alter lengths.

Across word boundaries

The usual reason a line that looks wrong is right. Tap ▶︎ to hear before → after.

How to type for best results:

The script hides short vowels, so the scanner considers every plausible reading and lets the meter choose, like a reader would. Two things help it: write tashdīd ّ where a letter is doubled (مدّت، قصّہ، امّید), and write zer ِ for an iẓāfat you'd pronounce (غمِ دل). Everything else is automatic.

About Baḥr

Sources, scanner accuracy, and academic acknowledgments.

How far to trust the scanner

Tested against the handbook's own answer key: on all 24 exercise ghazals (226 lines), Pritchett's meter fits 225 lines, and stacking names the right meter for 23 of 24 ghazals (the miss: Akbar's English "M.A.", which she scans unusually). On her printed syllable-by-syllable breakdown of Mir's Hindi-meter ghazal it matches 108 of 108 syllables.

Rules: Pritchett & Khaliq, chs. 1–3. Word lists verified against the same.

Make the rhythm with your own hand

Producing a rhythm trains the ear faster than hearing one. Tap once per syllable; hold a long twice as long as a short before the next tap.

Listen, then tap it back on the pad.

Recite a misra aloud and tap each syllable as you say it. Press Done when finished. I'll turn your taps into = and –, then check the bahr. The final syllable's length can't be heard from taps, so it stays flexible.
